text:
The first time the ceiling wept, it was in the Linguistics suite, directly over the photocopier, and Dr. Marguerite Aldous, who had been waiting for a syllabus to finish printing, stood and watched a single brown bead gather itself at the edge of an acoustic tile. It hung there with what she could only describe as deliberation. Then it dropped onto the paper tray, and the machine, in its fashion, carried on.

This was in October. The Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences had been in the Halvorsen Building for fourteen months, moved there from Victorian townhouses the university described as "no longer aligned with our strategic vision." The Halvorsen was aligned. It was glass and zinc, and it had won a sustainability prize from an organization whose acronym nobody could remember. At the opening, the Vice-Chancellor had called it "a building that breathes." Marguerite remembered thinking that people who said this about buildings had rarely been in one during a flu season.

The explanation arrived in an email from Facilities Management with the subject line "Minor Envelope Remediation." A waterproofing membrane, it said, meant to sit between the cladding and the structural wall, had been "omitted in certain zones during original construction." The word *omitted* was doing a great deal of work. Marguerite, who had spent thirty years teaching students that passive constructions conceal agents, pinned the email to her corkboard as a teaching aid. Nobody had omitted anything. It had simply been omitted.

The remediation began in November on the north façade, where the historians lived. The method involved removing the zinc panels in sections, exposing the bare wall, and applying the missing membrane by hand, in the rain, which several people noted was a peculiar way to waterproof something. Scaffolding went up, wrapped in blue mesh, and the historians found themselves working in aquarium light, with workmen's boots passing at the level of their desks and the occasional face appearing at the window with the mild, incurious expression of a man at a zoo.

"They can see my screen," said Desmond Pryce, the Head of History, who had lately taken to working with a cardboard box over his monitor, like a man guarding a small, bright animal.

"They're not interested in your screen," Marguerite said.

"That's what a spy would say."

The drilling started at seven. Facilities had promised that noisy work would be confined to "low-impact windows," a phrase that turned out to mean any period in which someone was trying to think. A seminar on Reconstruction was conducted by a graduate student who had to shout the word *amendment* over a pneumatic hammer, and who afterward developed a hoarseness the department secretary treated as an occupational injury. Someone circulated a spreadsheet to log the noise. By December it had four hundred entries and a tab labelled "Vibes."

Then there was the smell. It began in the second week of the work, a sweetish chemical note that the workmen called "just the primer" and that Marguerite identified as something like burnt almonds laid over a gym bag. By the third week it had settled into the ventilation, which, being a breathing building, shared it generously. Staff on the fourth floor reported headaches. A Sociology lecturer named Teodor, anxious and well-informed, reported a metallic taste and began carrying a handheld device that he claimed measured volatile organic compounds. It chirped. Everyone came to hate the chirp, and then, more disconcertingly, to ask what it said.

A meeting was called. It was held in the Brandt Room, the one space in the building that had never leaked, and which had therefore acquired the status of a shrine. A woman from Facilities, whose lanyard bore the title Senior Stakeholder Liaison, stood at the front with a slide that said WE HEAR YOU.

"We want to assure you," she began, "that the materials are fully compliant."

"With what?" said Desmond.

"With the relevant standards."

"Which are?"

She consulted her notes with a smile of such sustained pleasantness that Marguerite felt a flicker of pity. It could not be an easy thing, to be the human face of an omission. "I can follow up on that," the woman said.

Marguerite had once calculated that if every promise Facilities had made her since September were laid end to end, they would reach from her office to the building's front entrance, about ninety meters and a considerable amount of bad feeling.

Still, there were gestures. Air-quality tests were conducted, and the results were described as "within tolerance," a phrase Teodor's device made a public show of disputing. The Linguistics photocopier was moved to a dry location, and the ceiling over its former position was fitted with a plastic sheet, which collected water in a shallow bag and swelled over several days into a translucent udder. Someone drew a face on it. Someone else named it Gerald. For a week or two Gerald was a source of real morale, and when, one Thursday, the bag finally gave way and discharged itself onto the carpet, a small, sincere silence fell over the corridor, as at the death of a mascot.

By January the north façade was finished. The blue mesh came down, the zinc panels went back up, and the historians got their light again, which fell across their desks with an almost embarrassing generosity. Desmond removed the box from his monitor. For three days the building was quiet, and people walked its corridors with the careful, suspicious happiness of the recently discharged.

Then it rained, and the water came in on the south side.

A second email explained that the omission had not been confined to the north. The subject line was "Phase Two." The Faculty received this news like people told that the operation was a success but that there was, in fact, another leg. The south façade housed Sociology, Philosophy, and the Faculty's administrative core, and the scaffolding went up again over the winter break, so that students returning in February found the building wrapped in blue once more, like something being delivered.

Marguerite's office was on the south side. She had put off thinking about this, and now it arrived all at once: the hammer, the boots, the face at the window. The smell returned too, with a note of wet concrete. She moved her books to the middle shelves, away from the outer wall, and then, when a patch of black appeared behind the filing cabinet, moved them again, into boxes, which she stacked in the corridor with the others, so that the whole floor came to resemble a place from which people were about to be evacuated, or had been.

She wrote a letter. It was a good letter, measured and exact, the letter of a person who knew how to build an argument and had been given a great deal of material. She cited the spreadsheet, Teodor's device, the Vice-Chancellor's remark about breathing. Then she read it over and did not send it, because she could not think who would read it, or what they could do. The building was not going to be unbuilt. The people who had omitted the layer had long since moved on to other omissions, in other cities, and the people who remained were the ones who had to stay.

She understood, standing in the corridor among her boxes, that something had changed in her, and that it was not anger. It was closer to the feeling she had when a student's thesis, which had never been going to work, was finally allowed to fail: a loosening, a kind of grim tenderness. Nobody would be moved. The university had spent too much on the glass.

In March Facilities announced that the south façade would be complete by the end of the academic year, "weather permitting," and no one laughed, because by then they had learned that this was not a joke but a form of prayer. Desmond bought a dehumidifier for his office and, in solidarity, a second one for hers. Teodor stopped announcing the numbers, though he still carried the device, and sometimes Marguerite would see him glance at it in the stairwell and put it away without a word, like a man receiving news he had already guessed.

On the last Friday of term she stayed late. The workmen had gone, and the blue mesh lifted and settled against the windows in the wind, and the light in her office was the color of the inside of a shell. Somewhere above her a drop gathered, and fell, and she heard it land in the bucket she kept for the purpose, a small, clear note, like a question.

Next year, they had said, would be different: the building would finally be dry and bright and breathing. She did not entirely believe it. But she moved the bucket an inch to the left, put her syllabus in her bag, turned off the lamp, and went home, prepared, as one is for most things, to come back.
